value.misconception: A switch simply repeats every frame to all ports.
value.correction: A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and selectively forwards frames where forwarding state permits; hubs repeat traffic broadly.
Switch ports separate collision domains, but broadcasts are still forwarded within the broadcast domain.

value.misconception: Every network switch routes IP packets.
value.correction: Ordinary Ethernet switches commonly operate at Layer 2; Layer 3/multilayer switches add routing functionality.

value.misconception: MAC and IP addresses are interchangeable.
value.correction: MAC addresses guide link-layer forwarding; IP addresses support network-layer routing.

value.misconception: STP forwards on every redundant link.
value.correction: STP disables forwarding on selected links to create a loop-free active topology; SPB/TRILL are alternatives described as allowing multiple active paths.

value.misconception: A VLAN is a separate physical switch.
value.correction: A VLAN is logical Layer 2 segmentation that can be configured and tagged on managed switches.

value.misconception: Smart and enterprise switches have the same feature set.
value.correction: Smart switches offer limited features; enterprise switches provide broader configuration and monitoring capabilities.

value.misconception: Any device on a switch can sniff all switched traffic.
value.correction: Ordinary visibility is limited to relevant ports; port mirroring, taps, hubs or monitoring systems are used to observe additional traffic.

value.misconception: Cut-through waits for the entire frame before forwarding.
value.correction: Cut-through can begin forwarding after enough header data has arrived to make the decision.

value.misconception: PoE and UPS mean the same thing.
value.correction: PoE powers compatible endpoints over Ethernet; UPS backs up power to keep the switch and attached devices running during power loss.

value.misconception: The MAC table and CAM are exactly the same kind of thing.
value.correction: The MAC table is the logical mapping; CAM is a common high-speed hardware implementation.

value.misconception: Every switch port must use fiber modules.
value.correction: Switch interfaces can use different media; the source describes pluggable optics and DAC copper alternatives.

value.misconception: Full-duplex point-to-point links behave like shared half-duplex segments.
value.correction: The article says full-duplex has simultaneous transmit/receive and makes collisions impossible in the described model.

value.misconception: A managed switch by itself guarantees network security.
value.correction: ACLs, MAC filtering, 802.1X, VLANs, firewall and IDS integrations are features or controls, not a universal security guarantee.

value.misconception: Every internal switch hardware detail is explicitly specified by the article.
value.correction: CAM and transceivers/CPO are mentioned explicitly; detailed switch-fabric, ASIC pipeline and plane-separation descriptions are labeled engineering synthesis.

source_claims.claim: A network switch is a multiport bridge that forwards traffic toward destination devices, typically using MAC addresses at Layer 2.
Unlike a repeater hub, a switch learns device addresses and forwards data toward the destination port rather than repeating everything to all ports.
Each switch port forms a separate collision domain in the described Ethernet model, while broadcasts remain within the broadcast domain.
Switches may use SFP and other pluggable transceiver modules, DAC cables and co-packaged optics.
Some switches add Layer 3 routing and are called Layer 3 or multilayer switches.
The MAC address table maps MAC addresses to ports and is often implemented with high-speed CAM.
Cut-through switches may begin forwarding before the entire frame payload has arrived, reducing latency.
STP disables forwarding on selected links to avoid switching loops; SPB and TRILL are described as alternatives supporting active paths.
PoE can power endpoints such as VoIP phones and wireless access points; UPS-backed switch power can support continuity.
Managed switch features include VLANs, link aggregation, QoS, ACLs, SNMP, port mirroring, NTP, 802.1X, LLDP and IGMP snooping.
Port mirroring sends a copy of selected traffic to a monitoring port; alternatives include SMON, RMON, sFlow, a network tap or a Layer 1 hub.
The article credits Mark Kempf/DEC with the 1983 MAC bridge and dates Kalpana's seven-port EtherSwitch to 1989–1990.
The article warns that its lead may be too technical for most readers.

misconceptions.misconception: A switch simply repeats every frame to all ports.
misconceptions.correction: A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and selectively forwards frames where forwarding state permits; hubs repeat traffic broadly.
Switch ports separate collision domains, but broadcasts are still forwarded within the broadcast domain.

misconceptions.misconception: Every network switch routes IP packets.
misconceptions.correction: Ordinary Ethernet switches commonly operate at Layer 2; Layer 3/multilayer switches add routing functionality.

misconceptions.misconception: MAC and IP addresses are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: MAC addresses guide link-layer forwarding; IP addresses support network-layer routing.

misconceptions.misconception: STP forwards on every redundant link.
misconceptions.correction: STP disables forwarding on selected links to create a loop-free active topology; SPB/TRILL are alternatives described as allowing multiple active paths.

misconceptions.misconception: A VLAN is a separate physical switch.
misconceptions.correction: A VLAN is logical Layer 2 segmentation that can be configured and tagged on managed switches.

misconceptions.misconception: Smart and enterprise switches have the same feature set.
misconceptions.correction: Smart switches offer limited features; enterprise switches provide broader configuration and monitoring capabilities.

misconceptions.misconception: Any device on a switch can sniff all switched traffic.
misconceptions.correction: Ordinary visibility is limited to relevant ports; port mirroring, taps, hubs or monitoring systems are used to observe additional traffic.

misconceptions.misconception: Cut-through waits for the entire frame before forwarding.
misconceptions.correction: Cut-through can begin forwarding after enough header data has arrived to make the decision.

misconceptions.misconception: PoE and UPS mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: PoE powers compatible endpoints over Ethernet; UPS backs up power to keep the switch and attached devices running during power loss.

misconceptions.misconception: The MAC table and CAM are exactly the same kind of thing.
misconceptions.correction: The MAC table is the logical mapping; CAM is a common high-speed hardware implementation.

misconceptions.misconception: Every switch port must use fiber modules.
misconceptions.correction: Switch interfaces can use different media; the source describes pluggable optics and DAC copper alternatives.

misconceptions.misconception: Full-duplex point-to-point links behave like shared half-duplex segments.
misconceptions.correction: The article says full-duplex has simultaneous transmit/receive and makes collisions impossible in the described model.

misconceptions.misconception: A managed switch by itself guarantees network security.
misconceptions.correction: ACLs, MAC filtering, 802.1X, VLANs, firewall and IDS integrations are features or controls, not a universal security guarantee.

misconceptions.misconception: Every internal switch hardware detail is explicitly specified by the article.
misconceptions.correction: CAM and transceivers/CPO are mentioned explicitly; detailed switch-fabric, ASIC pipeline and plane-separation descriptions are labeled engineering synthesis.

value.expression: source → build → .next → static HTML → cache → browser

value.description: page_request → required_code_only

value.label: Serverless execution

value.label: Development update loop
value.description: code_change → detect → rerender/replace_module → browser

value.label: Incremental regeneration
value.description: static_output + later_regeneration
value.meaning: ISR extends static generation with incremental regeneration.

value.label: Routing
value.description: URL/path → routing_system → page/component
value.meaning: Next.js provides page-based and dynamic routing plus App Router.

value.label: Security update chain
value.description: vulnerability → CVE → affected_versions → fix_package → updated_version
value.meaning: Source describes a React vulnerability propagating downstream to Next.js and being fixed through an npm package.

value.label: Server-side vs client-side rendering
value.description: Server rendering occurs before content is sent to the browser; traditional React client rendering occurs in the browser.

value.label: Static vs dynamic rendering
value.description: Static output is built/cached ahead of requests; interactive/changing sites may not fit pure static generation.

value.label: SSR vs ISR
value.description: SSR renders on the server; ISR retains static output while supporting incremental regeneration.

value.label: App Router vs page-based routing
value.description: App Router is the newer routing architecture with layouts/RSC/streaming; page-based routing is the older routing model described by the source.

value.label: Webpack vs Turbopack
value.description: Webpack was the established bundler; Turbopack is described as its successor/replacement.

value.label: Compiler/transpiler vs bundler
value.description: SWC transforms/compiles code while Webpack/Turbopack bundle modules.

value.label: Code splitting vs prefetching
value.description: Code splitting reduces shipped code; prefetching anticipates resources to reduce load time.

value.label: Hot reload vs HMR
value.description: Both provide rapid development updates; HMR specifically replaces modules live.

value.label: Node/server vs browser runtime
value.description: Next.js spans server/runtime execution and browser delivery rather than being purely client-side.

value.label: Serverless vs self-deployment
value.description: Serverless uses on-demand functions; self-deployment is separately supported.

value.label: Next.js vs React
value.description: React is the underlying UI library; Next.js is a framework adding application architecture and rendering/deployment capabilities.

value.label: Edge runtime vs traditional server rendering
value.description: Edge capabilities are a deployment/runtime feature; server rendering is an application rendering model.

value.label: Framework vs toolchain
value.description: Next.js is the framework; Turbo/Turbopack/Turborepo are supporting development/build tools.

value.label: Vulnerability vs remediation
value.description: CVE records identify vulnerabilities; fix-react2shell-next is the remediation package described by the source.

value.label: Next.js is just React
value.description: Next.js is described as a full-stack framework built around React, adding server/static rendering, routing, data fetching, bundling and deployment capabilities.

value.label: Next.js only renders on the server
value.description: Next.js supports server rendering, static rendering, and client-side React behavior.

value.label: Static generation works for every site

value.label: SSR and static generation are identical

value.label: App Router was always the Next.js routing system

value.label: Turbopack and SWC do the same thing

value.label: Hot reload means the server must restart

value.description: The source documents a progression from page routing/server rendering through App Router, RSC, streaming, Rust tooling and Build Adapters.

source_claims.label: Rendering

source_claims.label: Development history
source_claims.description: The source documents releases from 2016 through 2026 and a progression of routing, rendering, tooling and deployment capabilities.

semantic_distinctions.label: Server-side vs client-side rendering
semantic_distinctions.description: Server rendering occurs before content is sent to the browser; traditional React client rendering occurs in the browser.

semantic_distinctions.label: Static vs dynamic rendering
semantic_distinctions.description: Static output is built/cached ahead of requests; interactive/changing sites may not fit pure static generation.

semantic_distinctions.label: SSR vs ISR
semantic_distinctions.description: SSR renders on the server; ISR retains static output while supporting incremental regeneration.

semantic_distinctions.label: App Router vs page-based routing
semantic_distinctions.description: App Router is the newer routing architecture with layouts/RSC/streaming; page-based routing is the older routing model described by the source.

semantic_distinctions.label: Webpack vs Turbopack
semantic_distinctions.description: Webpack was the established bundler; Turbopack is described as its successor/replacement.

semantic_distinctions.label: Compiler/transpiler vs bundler
semantic_distinctions.description: SWC transforms/compiles code while Webpack/Turbopack bundle modules.

semantic_distinctions.label: Code splitting vs prefetching
semantic_distinctions.description: Code splitting reduces shipped code; prefetching anticipates resources to reduce load time.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hot reload vs HMR
semantic_distinctions.description: Both provide rapid development updates; HMR specifically replaces modules live.

semantic_distinctions.label: Node/server vs browser runtime
semantic_distinctions.description: Next.js spans server/runtime execution and browser delivery rather than being purely client-side.

semantic_distinctions.label: Serverless vs self-deployment
semantic_distinctions.description: Serverless uses on-demand functions; self-deployment is separately supported.

semantic_distinctions.label: Next.js vs React
semantic_distinctions.description: React is the underlying UI library; Next.js is a framework adding application architecture and rendering/deployment capabilities.

semantic_distinctions.label: Edge runtime vs traditional server rendering
semantic_distinctions.description: Edge capabilities are a deployment/runtime feature; server rendering is an application rendering model.

semantic_distinctions.label: Framework vs toolchain
semantic_distinctions.description: Next.js is the framework; Turbo/Turbopack/Turborepo are supporting development/build tools.

semantic_distinctions.label: Vulnerability vs remediation
semantic_distinctions.description: CVE records identify vulnerabilities; fix-react2shell-next is the remediation package described by the source.

misconceptions.label: Next.js is just React

misconceptions.description: Next.js supports server rendering, static rendering, and client-side React behavior.

misconceptions.label: Static generation works for every site
misconceptions.description: The source explicitly notes static output is not suitable for every site, particularly highly interactive sites with frequent changes/user input.

misconceptions.label: SSR and static generation are identical
misconceptions.description: The source distinguishes server-side rendering from build-time static generation and caching.

misconceptions.label: App Router was always the Next.js routing system
misconceptions.description: App Router was introduced in Next.js 13 and stabilized in 13.4.

misconceptions.label: Turbopack and SWC do the same thing
misconceptions.description: SWC is described as a transpiler/compiler; Turbopack is a bundler.

misconceptions.label: Hot reload means the server must restart
misconceptions.description: Hot reloading is specifically described as avoiding server restart while reflecting code changes.

misconceptions.label: Next.js cannot deploy without Vercel

misconceptions.label: Next.js 13.4 only added another experimental router

misconceptions.label: Server rendering automatically makes every application secure

misconceptions.label: Next.js versions have no architectural evolution
misconceptions.description: The source documents a progression from page routing/server rendering through App Router, RSC, streaming, Rust tooling and Build Adapters.

value.title: nginx — Full-detail knowledge graph
value.description: A source-grounded, machine-readable graph of nginx, its features, protocols, architecture, ecosystem, history, licensing, comparative notes and implementation considerations.
value.scope: Based on the user-provided Wikipedia article text. Inferences are explicitly labeled.

value.name: Edge reverse proxy
value.description: Clients connect to nginx, which terminates or handles HTTP-level traffic and forwards requests to upstream application services.
value.source_basis: Core reverse-proxy role is explicit; detailed deployment flow is a generalized architecture interpretation.

value.name: Static content delivery
value.description: nginx serves static files, index files and optionally auto-indexed directory listings.

value.name: Load-balanced application
value.description: nginx distributes incoming requests across backend servers and can use in-band health checks.
value.source_basis: Load balancing and in-band health checks are explicitly listed.

value.name: Reverse proxy with HTTP caching
value.description: nginx caches eligible responses so repeated requests can be served without always querying the backend.
value.source_basis: Caching is explicit; exact cache policy and bypass rules are not covered in the supplied article.

value.name: Dynamic application integration
value.description: nginx serves as a front end for dynamic content through FastCGI, SCGI, uWSGI, WSGI application servers or Phusion Passenger.

value.name: TLS-enabled frontend
value.description: nginx supports TLS/SSL features such as SNI, OCSP stapling and TLS protocol integrations; a frontend TLS termination topology is a common inference.
value.source_basis: TLS/SSL features are explicit; exact termination topology is inferred.

value.name: Mail protocol proxy
value.description: nginx can proxy SMTP, POP3 and IMAP, with TLS/SSL and STARTTLS; authentication is delegated to an external HTTP server or script.
value.source_basis: Protocol and authentication features are explicit.

value.name: Graceful configuration or executable upgrade
value.description: The article states nginx can upgrade its executable and configuration without losing client connections.
value.source_basis: Explicitly listed feature; operational procedure is not detailed in the supplied article.

value.name: Containerized web frontend
value.description: nginx is commonly deployed in Docker containers according to a 2018 usage survey; container orchestration details are outside the source.
value.source_basis: The source reports a historical survey finding, not a current universal deployment statistic.

value.name: Commercial API gateway and management
value.description: NGINX Plus API gateway functionality was associated with NGINX Controller, announced as an API management tool in 2017.
value.source_basis: Commercial product relationship is explicit; flow is conceptual.

value.rule: For high numbers of concurrent connections, nginx's asynchronous event-driven approach is a core architectural choice.
value.rationale: The article contrasts its event-driven model with thread-based handling and connects it to predictable performance under high load.

value.rule: Do not assume nginx natively supports Apache-style .htaccess per-file overrides.
value.rationale: The article explicitly identifies this as a flexibility difference.

value.rule: Verify third-party module compatibility and build requirements before deploying modules.
value.rationale: The article notes modules may need to be compiled alongside nginx, may not all support dynamic loading, and some still require static linking.

value.rule: Treat the article's HTTP/3 status as experimental from nginx 1.25.0, not as a blanket statement about every build or later release.
value.rationale: The source specifically characterizes HTTP/3 as experimental starting with version 1.25.0.

value.rule: Encrypted Client Hello support depends on using a compatible OpenSSL branch and the relevant nginx build/configuration.
value.rationale: The source conditions ECH support on nginx 1.29.4 and an OpenSSL branch implementing ECH.

value.rule: Plan an external HTTP service or authentication script for nginx mail-proxy authentication.
value.rationale: The source says mail proxy authentication requires an external HTTP server or script.

value.rule: Do not assume NGINX Unit receives upstream maintenance after October 2025.
value.rationale: The article says it was archived by maintainers and is no longer receiving updates.

architecture_patterns.description: Clients connect to nginx, which terminates or handles HTTP-level traffic and forwards requests to upstream application services.

architecture_patterns.name: Static content delivery
architecture_patterns.description: nginx serves static files, index files and optionally auto-indexed directory listings.

architecture_patterns.source_basis: Load balancing and in-band health checks are explicitly listed.

architecture_patterns.name: Reverse proxy with HTTP caching

architecture_patterns.name: Dynamic application integration
